# RFC-0006: Rendering: component boundaries, surface and overlay

> **Version:** 0.1.0 | **Status:** draft | **Phase:** spec
> **Owners:** @wael
> **Tags:** `architecture`, `out-of-core`, `gui`

---

## 1. Summary

### [RFC-0006:C-OVERVIEW] Overview and scope (Informative) <a id="rfc-0006c-overview"></a>

Two things determine whether a viewport is usable: what the renderer is allowed to depend on, and what may be
drawn over it. Both are constraints from outside the renderer rather than choices within it — one imposed by
licensing and adoption, the other by the fact that composited content carries no depth.

**Scope** — the dependency direction between components and the latency guarantee of the rendering data path;
what the renderer accepts from its host; where a graphical toolkit may appear; and which content must be
drawn by the renderer rather than composited over it.

**Out of scope** — the rendering algorithm, level-of-detail selection and the node cache. Interface layout
and tool design. The render synchronisation boundary, which belongs with editing ([RFC-0007:C-EXTRACT](../rfc/RFC-0007.md#rfc-0007c-extract)).
Caching ([RFC-0004](../rfc/RFC-0004.md)).

C-LAYERING is here for one reason only: its item 3 fixes the direction dependencies run, and the direction
that matters is the one that keeps the spatial access layer adoptable *without* the renderer. Its items 1 and
2 — the prohibition on a general-purpose query engine — are a data-layer constraint whose argument belongs to
the operator contract, and they sit here because splitting a three-item clause across two RFCs would cost
more than the misfit does. That is a judgement, not a claim that they are rendering concerns.

---

## 2. Specification

### [RFC-0006:C-LAYERING] Component layering and the query-engine boundary (Normative) <a id="rfc-0006c-layering"></a>

A general-purpose query engine's physical-operator interface is a large surface on its own release
cadence. Depending on it means absorbing that churn permanently, in the components whose own public
traits are least settled — and putting a throughput-oriented planner where C-RENDER needs a frame
budget.

1. The spatial access, operator, and rendering components MUST NOT depend, directly or transitively, on a
   general-purpose SQL query engine.
   - Compliance MUST be verified against the resolved dependency graph, not by review alone.
2. If a SQL interface over point cloud data is provided, it MUST be a separate optional component that
   depends on the spatial access layer.
   - The spatial access layer MUST NOT depend on it.
3. The spatial access component MUST NOT depend on the operator component or the rendering component.
   - The operator component MUST NOT depend on the rendering component.

#### Rationale

This clause constrains the dependency graph, not the feature set. The direction stated in (2) is what
preserves the option: exposing a settled spatial access layer to a query engine later is straightforward,
whereas extracting an engine dependency from underneath established traits is a rewrite.

Most point cloud operations *are* ordinary special cases of the tabular model. The two that are not are
overlapping partitions ([RFC-0002:C-HALO](../rfc/RFC-0002.md#rfc-0002c-halo) 2) and level of detail, and those two are the product — the full
assessment is recorded in the accompanying architecture decision rather than here.

(3) keeps the spatial access component adoptable on its own. C-RENDER 1 has the renderer read it
directly, which makes merging the two look attractive — they are adjacent and one is nearly a consumer of
the other. Separation is what allows a tool with its own renderer, or none, to take the spatial access
layer without inheriting a graphics dependency.

Separation constrains dependency, not influence. The spatial access component is expected to be *shaped
by* what the renderer needs — cancellable requests, level-of-detail selection, a useful eviction policy —
because C-RENDER 1 makes the renderer its most latency-sensitive consumer. The requirement is that the
arrow points one way, not that the two are designed apart.

### [RFC-0006:C-RENDER] Rendering data path (Normative) <a id="rfc-0006c-render"></a>

Planning latency is a function of pipeline complexity, which the user controls and which is unbounded. A
viewport is latency-bound by the frame it must service. Coupling the two gives a viewport that stalls
precisely when the camera is moving.

1. The rendering data path MUST obtain point data from the spatial access layer directly, without
   traversing the operator planner.
2. A rendering data request MUST be cancellable.
   - Cancellation MUST take effect without waiting for already-dispatched work on that request to run to
     completion.
3. Displaying the output of a processing pipeline MUST be a separately scheduled operation, and MUST NOT
   be performed synchronously by the rendering data path.
4. Frame scheduling MUST belong to the host rather than to the renderer.
   - What the renderer may not do in service of that — own a thread, block on presentation, block on device
     work — is stated once, at C-SURFACE 3.

#### Rationale

Cancellability (2) is required because camera motion invalidates in-flight requests faster than they
complete; a path that can only be waited on accumulates obsolete work until it collapses. Requiring
cancellation to take effect *without draining* dispatched work is the substantive part — a cancellation
that must first finish what it started is not useful at frame rate.

(3) is what (1) would otherwise leave ambiguous. Nothing here prohibits showing processed results; the
prohibition is on the render path doing the processing inline, which would reintroduce exactly the
unbounded latency (1) removes.

(4) states only *whose* the frame loop is, and defers the prohibitions to C-SURFACE 3 rather than repeating
them. Three normative statements of one obligation — here, C-SURFACE 3, and [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) 3 and 4 —
with divergent prohibition lists would give a compliance checker two answers about whether blocking on
device work is in scope. The connection worth keeping is why it matters here: a renderer blocked on
presentation cannot observe the cancellation (2) requires.

### [RFC-0006:C-TOOLKIT] Toolkit confinement (Normative) <a id="rfc-0006c-toolkit"></a>

A graphical toolkit is an application concern. Confining it there is required by licensing, and is also what
keeps the renderer usable by anything that is not this application.

1. A library crate MUST NOT depend, directly or transitively, on a graphical toolkit or on bindings to one.
   - Compliance MUST be verified against the resolved dependency graph, not by review alone.
2. The renderer MUST NOT contain code specific to any one toolkit or windowing system.
   - Toolkit-specific integration belongs to the application, which supplies the surface (C-SURFACE 1).

#### Rationale

(1) follows from [RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license) 4 — Qt's open-source terms are LGPL-3.0 and GPL-3.0, both beyond
`Apache-2.0 OR MIT` — but is stated separately because the architectural reason outlives the licensing one.
The commercial-licence loophole that would otherwise apply here (Qt is also sold commercially, so a
dependency could be argued compliant *for this project* while obliging every adopter) is closed generally by
[RFC-0001:C-LICENSE](../rfc/RFC-0001.md#rfc-0001c-license) 4's third sub-item rather than restated.

(2) is stated as a prohibition on *content* rather than as "implementable against any windowing system",
which would be a universal claim about systems nobody has built and so unfalsifiable. Absence of
toolkit-specific code is inspectable; universal implementability is not.

(2) is also the part that survives if licensing ever changes. A renderer that knows which toolkit is hosting it
cannot be adopted by a tool using a different one, and adoption by other tools is the entire purpose of
publishing these crates permissively. The verification requirement in (1) exists because the failure mode is
identical to a licence violation — a toolkit dependency pulled in transitively by a convenience crate breaks
nothing visible and is found by no test.

### [RFC-0006:C-SURFACE] Host-supplied render surface (Normative) <a id="rfc-0006c-surface"></a>

The renderer draws into a surface it is given and does not know what produced it. This is the same
arrangement [RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) applies to storage and retrieval, extended to presentation.

1. The renderer MUST accept its drawing target as an opaque native surface handle supplied by its host.
2. The renderer MUST NOT create, own, or manage a window.
   - It MUST NOT depend on the surface having been produced by any particular toolkit or windowing system.
3. The renderer MUST NOT own a thread, block on presentation, or block on device work
   ([RFC-0004:C-HOST](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-host) 3 and 4).
   - Frame scheduling belongs to the host (C-RENDER 4).
4. The renderer MUST also accept a target it does not present directly — an offscreen target whose result
   the host composites.
   - Switching between presenting and offscreen operation MUST NOT change the obligations in (1) to (3).

#### Rationale

(1) and (2) keep the renderer toolkit-agnostic as C-TOOLKIT 2 requires, and are cheap because a native
surface handle is what every windowing system already exposes. It is also what a browser canvas exposes, so
this satisfies [RFC-0004:C-PORT-GATE](../rfc/RFC-0004.md#rfc-0004c-port-gate) without a second code path.

(3) is where this differs from an ordinary embedded renderer, which would spawn a render thread and block on
presentation. Neither is available: the renderer must compile with no threads and must not block, so it is a
function from state to drawn output rather than a loop.

(4) is forward compatibility that is nearly free now and expensive later. Presenting directly to a surface
defers all graphics-interop work; compositing an offscreen result into a toolkit's scene graph is what
C-OVERLAY 2 will eventually require. Because rendering into a host-composited target is a superset of
presenting to a surface, admitting both from the outset means the later transition changes the application
and not the renderer's published contract.

### [RFC-0006:C-OVERLAY] Depth correctness and overlay content (Normative) <a id="rfc-0006c-overlay"></a>

Content composited over the viewport by a toolkit has no depth information, so it cannot be occluded by the
point cloud. Whether that is acceptable depends entirely on the content, and the line is worth fixing before
the first label is drawn.

1. Content whose correctness depends on depth relative to the point cloud MUST be drawn by the renderer.
   - This includes measurements anchored to points, annotations attached to positions, and selection
     geometry in the scene.
   - A host MUST NOT composite such content over the viewport.
2. Content independent of scene depth MAY be composited over the viewport by the host.
   - This includes tool palettes, panels, readouts, and other interface chrome.

#### Rationale

A label composited on top of the viewport floats in front of geometry it should be behind. For a measurement
anchored to a point on the far side of a stand, that is not a cosmetic flaw: the reading appears to belong to
the near surface, which is a different tree. Drawing it in the renderer is the only way it can be
depth-tested against the cloud.

The prohibition is nested under (1) rather than stated as a sibling because it obliges a different party for
the same reason — the renderer must draw it, therefore the host must not. Stating it explicitly matters
because the tempting shortcut runs the other way: drawing a text label with the toolkit is far easier than
drawing text in the renderer, and the result looks correct in every screenshot taken from a viewpoint where
nothing occludes it.

(2) records that the restriction is narrow. Interface chrome has no spatial relationship to the scene, so
compositing it is correct as well as convenient, and it is the reason offscreen compositing (C-SURFACE 4) is
worth supporting at all rather than keeping the viewport permanently opaque.
